items.t: Table of the expansion of the letters [harflerin basti cetveli] — columns right to left: letters [harfler]; greater abjad value [ebcedi Kabir]; the numbers written out in words [sayilarin yazilishi]; first, second, third, fourth and fifth expansion [birinci–beshinji basṭ]. [I 93]
Chapter 15 (al-bāb al-khāmis ʿashar): On the conditions binding upon some and not others, from the commencement of beginnings to the suns of endings [165]

Know — may God, exalted is He, grant me and you success in obedience to Him and in the understanding of the secrets of His blessed names — that God, glorified and exalted, created the angels who bear the Throne, who encompass the Footstool, who exercise disposal from the Pen, and who peruse the Preserved Tablet; and He appointed for them kinds of litanies of remembrance and differing acts of devotion, and likewise for the inhabitants of the heavens. Except that the people of the Highest Assembly, who are the people of the Throne — their litany of remembrance is Quddūs Quddūs (All-Holy, All-Holy); whereas the people of the Footstool — their litany of remembrance is Subbūḥ

Quddūs (All-Glorified, All-Holy), Lord of the angels and the Spirit. And know that among the meanings of His name al-Quddūs (the All-Holy) is that God, exalted is He, discloses to the one who utters it, in his wayfaring within the Omnipotence (jabarūt), the subtleties of the highest Omnipotence. And in this Omnipotence are the Lote-Tree of the Boundary (sidrat al-muntahā), the holy Presence of intimate converse, the luminous veils, the seas of lights, the highest rafraf, the pavilions (surādiqāt) of the intellects, the science of the combinatory letters, and the terminus of the realities. These are the eight. The eight are the Throne, the Footstool, the Pen, the Tablet, and the Highest Assembly — exalted are His lights above the cognitive apprehensions. Now among the occult properties of His name al-Quddūs is that al-Subbūḥis joined to it, so that you say SubbūḥQuddūs; for then there is unveiled to him the highest Dominion (malakūt). And in the highest Dominion are the Dominion, the Omnipotence, the highest kingdom (mulk), the Level (al-mustawā), the Tablets and the Pens /fol. 114r./ — this according to his word, upon him be blessing and peace: ((I reached the Level until I heard the scratching of the Pens.)) And among the occult properties of His name al-Quddūs al-Subbūḥ, Lord of the angels and the Spirit, is that this be disclosed to him. And the lower Dominion — within it are eight: the Footstool and the seven heavens; and the lower Omnipotence — within it are the seven earths; and the kingdom — within it are eight: heat, moisture, cold, dryness, the inanimate, the animal, the plant, and the mineral. And this litany of remembrance is the litany of the bearers of the Throne, and it is the litany of the Holy Spirit — peace be upon him — who is a mighty angel, than whom God, exalted is He, created none greater after the Throne; and he is the master of inspiration. And it is said that he is Gabriel — peace be upon him — who is the very reality of the sending down of revelation, according to His word, exalted is He: Say: the Holy Spirit brought it down (Q 16:102). And this litany of remembrance is likewise the litany of the chiefs of the angels, the people of the Highest Assembly. So sanctification gathers the lights of sanctification and the Holy Spirit. In the Presence of the Holy Spirit is holiness (al-quds), and it manifests itself through the realities of faith within pure hearts; and it is the revelation of inspiration; and this holy Presence is at the Lote-Tree of the Boundary. And al-quds is that which is declared transcendent above defects. Nay, I say: al-quds is that which is declared transcendent above every description of perfection which created beings suppose to be a perfection of their own attributes, and above the fact that the ignorant man and the blind man and others are deficient in their very essence. So declare God, exalted is He, transcendent of whatever they know of their own qualities.

And know that the healing treasure of divine oneness and its pure drinking-place lies only in Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣand in what accords with it; and for that reason it equals a third of the Qurʾān. For the Qurʾān comprises narratives, legal rulings, and the affirmation of oneness. So take the exposition of it and the understanding of its secret from the standpoint of rational consideration. And we abridge from its meanings and the choicest of its jewels that which is most radiant to the eyes and highest in outward aspect and in inward report. I say — and from God comes help — the word of the Real: "Say: He". He is the one whose ipseity (huwiyya) belongs to His own essence; and He is necessary of existence, and His existence is the very same as His quiddity (māhiyya). So the Necessary of Existence is the one of whom [it is said]: there is no god but He; and He is the one whose ipseity belongs to His own essence: He is He; nay, His essence is that He is He and no other. So that ipseity and that particularity is a meaning devoid of name. And that is the being of that divinity a god; for the god is that to which what is other than it is related, while He Himself is not related to another. And the absolute God is the one who is such with respect to all existents. The relation of what is other than Him to Him is relational (iḍāfī), whereas His being unrelated to another is negative (salbī). And since the divine ipseity is such as cannot be expressed, by reason of its majesty and its immensity, save by saying that He is He, He said "Say: He". Then we expound that ipseity; and it can only be expounded by its necessary concomitants (lawāzim). And of the concomitants, some are relational and some negative; and the relational is more productive of ramification than the negative. /fol. 114v./ And the most complete in operative deployment is the concomitant that gathers both kinds, the relational and the negative; and that is the being of that ipseity a god. Hence necessarily He followed His word "He" with the mention of "God", exalted is He, so that "God" should be as an unveiler of what the word "He" indicates, and as an exposition of it. And among them is this: that when He had expounded that ipseity by its divine concomitants, He followed that with His being "the One", which is the utmost limit of oneness. For divinity is the utmost limit in unity and in the perfection of its spreading out — a limit of which the intellects fall short of laying hold, and short even of standing below the first beginnings of the shining forth of its lights. Glory be to Him! How immense is His affair, and how overpowering His authority! For He is the one who is the ultimate term of all needs, and from whom comes the attainment of all requests. The least of what He has reserved to Himself of majesty and immensity and felicity is not reached by the utmost of the descriptions of those who describe, nor by the greatest description of the describers. Rather, the measure that it is possible to mention is that beyond which more is impossible; and it is what He mentioned in His mighty Book: Is there any doubt concerning God?(Q 14:10). And this is because His quiddity, blessed and exalted is He — although it is impossible for any other than He to know it save by the intermediary of relation — He, mighty and majestic, is the Knower of it. For this reason He did not mention that quiddity, and confined Himself to those concomitants.

So we say: the First Principle has nothing whatever of premises at all; for His oneness is sheer, there is no multiplicity in Him, and there is no whereness (ayniyya) there at all. Thus we know no premises of His essence; rather we know of His essence nothing but a pure, unmixed ipseity, declared transcendent of multiplicity in every respect. And those respects have concomitants. So when the ipseity is mentioned and expounded by the near concomitants rather than the remote ones, that gives notice of the absence of premises; for if He had premises He would not be necessary by His own essence, and His existence would be dependent upon them. And His word "One" is a hyperbole in unity, which is realized only when the unity is such that there can be nothing more intense nor more complete than it. For "the one" is predicated of what falls under it by modulation (tashkīk); and so that which is not divisible in any respect at all is more entitled to oneness than that which is divisible in some respects. And the proof of it is that everything which has things falling under its ipseity comes to be only from the conjoining of parts, its ipseity being dependent upon the presence of those parts, so that it is not an ipseity by virtue of its own essence — as is indicated by His word, exalted is He: Say: He is God, One (Q 112:1). Therefore He has nothing of parts. For this reason He turned aside from the concomitants. And His word al-Ṣamad, the Eternal Refuge (Q 112:2) has two interpretations in the language: one of them, that which has no hollow interior; the second, the Lord. The first is negative, an indication of the divine Self; for everything that has a quiddity has a hollow and an inward, and that is that quiddity, whereas that which has no inward yet is existent is the God. And there is no consideration in His essence save existence stripped bare of restrictions. And according to the second interpretation its meaning is relational, namely His being the Lord of all, the Beginner of all; and it may be that to be such is for all to stand in need of Him while He stands in need of no other. And His word, exalted is He, /fol. 115r./ He did not beget and was not begotten (Q 112:3): when He, exalted is He, had made clear that all is supported upon Him, and that He is the one who gives all existents their existence, and that He is the One who overflows upon all existents, He, glorified is He, made clear that it is impossible that one like Him should be generated from Him. For everyone from whom one like him is generated — his quiddity is shared between him and another, for he is individuated only by the intermediary of matter and its attachment, and by designation and restriction. Everything that is material, or that has an attachment to matter, is generated from another. So the sense of the words comes to be thus: He did not beget (Q 112:3), because He is not generated. And since He has neither quiddity nor [any other] consideration, it becomes clear that He is He — and it is with the mention of Him that He began at the opening of the sura — and that His ipseity belongs to His own essence, and in that He is not generated from another. And had His ipseity been acquired from another, He would not be He by His own essence. And in this there is an alerting to a mighty secret, namely the threat that occurs in the Qurʾān against him who asserts a son and a consort. We return to this secret: it is that the offspring is separated off if its specific quiddity be not made multiple, and the cause of that is matter, as we have explained. And everything that is material — its quiddity is not an ipseity. Therefore no other is generated from Him, and He is not generated from another. His word, exalted is He, and none is equal to Him (Q 112:4): that is, He has nothing that equals Him in the strength of existence. As for His having something that equals Him in specific quiddity, that is refuted by His word, exalted is He, He did not beget and was not begotten (Q 112:3); for every quiddity that is shared between Him and another — its existence would be material, and it would be generated from another.

Faṣl. The discourse in it bears upon the preponderance of the formula There is no god but Godover all other formulae; and I make clear the excellence of Say: He is God, One (Q 112:1) and of the Throne Verse (Q 2:255) over all other suras and verses; and I make clear the reality of oneness within them — until he said: And I shall make clear to you the secrets of what you long for, and shall unfurl thereby your banners toward the Highest Companion, and your ease toward the tents pitched upon the margins of al-ʿAqīq and al-Ḥimā, and toward the domes that lie near the side of "two bows' length or nearer", where the majesty of There is no god but God— nay, of There is no god but He— has been established. It is a door that is opened only to the yearning ones who come to it; and short of its heights the eyes of the beholders and the understandings of created beings, all of them, are veiled. For not every secret may be divulged, nor may every connection be made to grow and to spring up; rather, the breasts of the free are the graves of secrets. And the divulging of the secret of Lordship is unbelief, a thing well known among those who possess knowledge of God, exalted is He. And if the divulging of the secret of Lordship is unbelief, then the divulging of the secret of the withness (maʿiyya) and of the ipseity and of union is more thoroughgoing in entailing unbelief, and more emphatic. Nor is it hidden from the learned that what gives rise to unbelief is the depositing of the secrets with one who has no fitness for them. To this the Messenger of God — God bless him

— and grant him peace, when he said: ((Among knowledge there is that which is like a thing treasured up and hidden away: none knows it /fol. 115v./ save those who know God and he who loves Him passionately.)) So hear, O you who yearn: were you to efface your existence and annihilate it, and to depart from yourself and from your seeing, and were your seeing to depart from you and from all that is other than Him and other than you, then the secret of the breaths to which allusion has been made would be unveiled to you. For in your saying "No" while your existence yet remains there is a rational self-contradiction and an unbelief in the way of passionate love. So understand, and you will attain the secret of the marvellous indication. Now as for the second — namely illā ("save") — it is that by which and in which there breaks the dawn of intimacy and of unveiling: the traces of pre-eternity (al-qidam) and of necessity (al-wujūb), from among the branches of the secrets. Illā is what delimits the ruling of divine singularity (fardāniyya) for those possessed of divine oneness, of the indications, and of the secrets. As for the beginnings of the first valley, they are lā ("no"); and the beginnings of the second valley are ālāʾ (the divine bounties). In the first there flows the torrent of realization (taḥqīq); from the second there grows the wellspring of refinement (tanqīḥ). He who drinks from the first valley is like Dhū l-Qarnayn, and he who drinks from the second valley is like al-Khaḍir — peace be upon him. The first is made ready for annihilation (fanāʾ), the second is made ready for subsistence (baqāʾ). The indication of the first is an indication of the kingdom (mulk), and the second is an indication of the Dominion (malakūt). The first is the Holy House, and the second is the house of divine unicity and of intimacy. Indeed I am God; there is no god but I (Q 20:14). God — there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting (Q 2:255). God — there is no god but He; to Him belong the Most Beautiful Names (Q 20:8). And He gives report of the aspects of illā Llāh ("save God"): Has the account of Moses come to you? When he saw a fire (Q 20:9–10). He confirmed the vision for him; then He let down over him the veil of concealment — the secrets of those who love one another — by His words, exalted is He, a fire (Q 20:10). And He said O Moses, indeed I am God (cf. Q 28:30 and Q 20:14); then He veiled [it] with the veil and said your Lord (Q 20:12). And the secret of this expansion and of the evidences is unveiled through the allusion to the secret of His words Indeed I am God; there is no god but I, so worship Me (Q 20:14). And He made the beginnings of the knot of union to be divine oneness, and the end of its sealing to be obedience.

I shall inform you by an indication pointing first to the knowledge of Him and second to the knowledge of what is other than Him, and [I shall tell you] the secret of the utterance in the indication addressed to you: that you disavow whatever is other than Him, so that you may attain the sweetness of the secrets from His words Indeed I am God (Q 20:14). For if you are not like Moses son of ʿImrān — peace be upon him — in the moment and in the attribute, you will not attain the sweetness of the Beloved's call, nor will you taste the savour of union with Him. Will you not take instruction from the words of Moses, when he was asked, "How did you know that the call of the Real was from Him?" and he said: "Because the sweetness of the call enraptured me and engrossed me, so that every part and every hair of me was straitened; for I was addressed by a call reaching me from every direction, and the pavilions of Might encompassed me, and the divine awe took possession of me, and so I knew that the address that reached me was from God, exalted is He. And I said: You are He who has never ceased to be and shall never cease to be; You are He with whom Moses has no station, nor any motion of speech in words, unless You cause him to subsist by Your subsistence and raise him up by Your raising, so that You are at once the Addresser and the Addressed." And in this same manner came the reports of the Messenger of God — God bless him and grant him peace — from God, exalted is He, in His words: ((My servant, I fell ill and you did not visit Me)). Indeed I am God (Q 20:14) in both states. Love Him who, when you fall ill, visits you, and when you sin, turns to you in forgiveness. And the quintessence of the indication is that you sever your self from you, by your abandoning /fol. 116r./ everything that severs you from your Beloved.

Make your heart His House, make your existence His Mecca and your witnessing the Sanctuary, and persist in your circumambulation about the House — a circumambulation in secret — and you will find God as [surely as] the existence of the House. And journey with Him, living, in the contemplation of al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm (the Living, the Self-

Subsisting). The sign of that is the exchanging of existence for Existence, the changing hues of the attributes, and the veiling of the states. In these indications there is that which points to the affirmation of the singularity of the God who transcends all beginnings and all ends. And [such is] the quintessence of the indication.

Faṣl. Know that among the occult properties of the Qurʾān is God bears witness that there is no god but He — and the angels, and those possessed of knowledge — upholding justice. There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise (Q 3:18). In this verse there are three meanings. The first is that with which God began concerning Himself, for Himself: it is the attestation by the Necessary of Existence of the necessity of existence. For the Necessary of Existence is [such] in pre-eternity, since it is impossible to posit that any other than He should be together with Him, whether in essence or in attributes; whereas the admissibility of His being together with what is other than He is in respect of attributes, not of essence — [and this] because of His magnificence and the majesty of His essence and of His attributes, which preclude that anything other than He should be together with Him. The second is the regard for that with which God made [His testimony] second, from among His angels, on account of their attestation of the state of existence as belonging to Him. That is an existential testimony and a knowledge by direct vision, in which the picturing of any wavering is impossible, because the angels are sanctified above the film of the carnal soul, the darknesses of form, and the seal of clay. And the third is that with which God made a third [testimony], from among His servants, describing them as possessed of knowledge and as upholders of justice, or as attesting Him; for sound attestation is valid only from one who knows. And Ibn ʿAbbās — may God be pleased with them both — said: the sense of the words is: God bore witness for Himself, even had none other than He borne witness for Him, that there is no god but He — and the angels (Q 3:18) bear witness to that for Him. And His words and those possessed of knowledge (Q 3:18) mean the prophets and the believers: they bear witness to that for Him. upholding justice (Q 3:18) — that is, with equity, because they are the people of equity; for the meaning of equity is the placing of a thing in its proper place, and that cannot be so save through knowledge. There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise (Q 3:18): the Mighty, [withholding] the blessing from him who does not believe in Him; the Wise, by what they have borne witness to of there is no god but He (Q 3:18), and that they should worship none but Him, and that the religion approved with God is Islam.

Faṣl. Know that the reality of the testimony to divine oneness is what the Real bore witness to for Himself, by Himself; for He is the witness of His own essence, and He called to witness those of His creation whom He called to witness, before He created them, so as to alert them that He knows what shall be. So His testimony for Himself, by that to which He bore witness, is a testimony of truth; and He informed creation that testimony is accepted only from the truthful ones who profess His oneness — those who would come, and would know Him, and would declare His oneness, and would bear witness to His divinity and His lordship — as in His words, exalted is He: God bears witness that there is no god but He — and the angels, and those possessed of knowledge — upholding justice. There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise (Q 3:18). Now the angels' testimony to that is a testimony of necessity, because of what they witness of the majesty of His kingship and the traces of His magnificence, for they were moulded upon that. Then He said and those possessed of knowledge (Q 3:18) — that is, the learned, who are the masters of the realities treasured up within the realities /fol. 116v./ of divine oneness; who point to the declaration of God's singularity (tafrīd); who give expression to the meanings of the [spiritual] states; who set themselves apart from all things for the One Alone (al-Fard); who declare the oneness of al-Aḥad al-Ṣamad (the One, the Eternally Besought); who know the meanings of the names of the Real and the realities of their attributes; and who behold the unseen realms with their own eyes. They are the proof of God, exalted is He, in the lands, and to them the servants have recourse. They have set down their travelling gear in the Presence, and their ranks have been raised in a seat of truth, with an all-powerful Sovereign (Q 54:55). And Ibn ʿAbbās — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with them both — said: God, exalted is He, bore this testimony two thousand years before He created creation. And in another report from him it is said: twelve thousand years, each year of them three hundred and sixty days, each day of them a thousand years of what you count. And what is transmitted from the Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ (the Brethren of Purity) is the abandoning of plunging into the sea of [discursive] indication, because it entails dispersion; rather, they must plunge into the seas of understanding and of the meanings when they hear the word of God, exalted is He, God bears witness (Q 3:18) — for it is a place of prostration, on account of the annihilation of existence — and they behold the world of witnessing, so as to realize existence through the Existence which has ordained the secrets within His ipseity: He is the First in the first and the Last in the last. Then, after that, [comes] the plunging into the sea of the secrets of there is no god but He (Q 3:18), for they are matters of [immediate] tasting (dhawq).

And know that the Mighty Qurʾān falls into three thirds: a third that indicates the knowledge of the essence of God, exalted is He, and of His attributes, His oneness, and His sanctity; a third that indicates the matters of the sacred Law; and the remaining third that indicates the knowledge of the matters of the hereafter. And there is no obscurity in this, that the indication which establishes the essence of God — mighty and majestic — and His attributes, under the description of necessity, of unicity, and of sanctity, equals the [other] two thirds of the Qurʾān, the two that indicate command and prohibition, promise and threat.

Faṣl. And know that the verses which are the Throne Verse comprise six attributes among the attributes of God, exalted is He — the attributes of divinity. The first of them is the negation of any partner, in His words There is no god but He (Q 2:255). The second is the affirmation of Life, which is the condition for the subsistence of all the other attributes of God, exalted is He: the Living (Q 2:255). And the third is the Self-

Subsisting (Q 2:255), concerning which Ibn ʿAbbās — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with them both — said: the One subsisting of Himself, who has no beginning — that is, the One subsisting through Himself, having no need of any other, having no need of substrate or of particularizer. And the fourth is the negation of defects from Him, in His words Neither slumber nor sleep overtakes Him (Q 2:255). And the fifth: He pointed to the perfection of divinity, in His words, exalted is He, To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth (Q 2:255) — that is, of creation and of command. And the sixth: He pointed to His sovereignty, in His words Who is there that shall intercede with Him save by His leave?(Q 2:255). As for His saying "God", it is the refutation of seven classes of the unbelievers: the eternalists (al-Dahriyya), the dualists, the worshippers of idols and of fires, the associators, the Jews, the Christians, and the Ṣābiʾa. As for His words God (Q 2:255), they are a refutation of the eternalists. And by His words there is no god but He (Q 2:255), a refutation of the dualists, and of those who assert a consort and a child, and of the Jews and the Christians. And by His words the Living (Q 2:255), a refutation of the worshippers of idols and of fires. And by His words the Self-Subsisting (Q 2:255), a refutation of the associators, and of him who asserts substrate, place, non-existence, and the divesting [of God of His attributes]. And by His words Neither slumber nor sleep overtakes Him (Q 2:255), /fol. 117r./ a refutation of the Jews and the Christians, and of those who assert the divinity of Jesus son of Mary and of ʿUzayr — [despite] the neediness of them both, and eating and drinking and sleeping and all the rest of the contingencies that may befall [them]. And by His words To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth (Q 2:255), a refutation of the Ṣābiʾa and of the worshippers of idols and of the stars, because the heavens and the earth and what is between them are created things. And by His words Who is there that shall intercede with Him save by His leave (Q 2:255) — a refutation of those who said, "We worship them only that they may bring us nearer to God in rank" (Q 39:3), and "These are our intercessors with God" (Q 10:18). And Salmān al-Fārisī — may God be pleased with him — related from the Prophet — God bless him and grant him peace — that he said: ((Whoever recites the Throne Verse, God, exalted is He, makes light for him the agonies of death. And the angels never pass by a house in which the Throne Verse is [to be found] but they are struck senseless; nor do they pass by "Say: He is God, One" (Q 112:1) but they prostrate; nor do they pass by the end of Sūrat al-Ḥashr but they fall upon their knees.))

Faṣl. The mark of one who has known God, exalted is He, with the gnosis that is His due: if you do not gain sight of his secret, no knowledge (ʿilm) of it is to be found. That is the gnosis beyond which there is no gnosis. And God, exalted is He, has favoured some men above others by the abiding presence of this state and by the absence of it.

Faṣl. If you desire that God, exalted is He, manifest to you the glimmerings of your own landmarks, then [guard] the bodily limbs from sloth, the soul from weariness, the intellect from wrangling, the heart from stumbling, the spirit from [long] hoping, and the innermost secret (sirr) from regarding the work, and from ascribing to itself the state and the locus.

Faṣl. The rule of realization (taḥqīq): there is nothing in the [symbolic] indication (ishāra) save God-given success. Whomever God wishes to guide, He expands his breast for Islam (Q 6:125), and He makes easy his affair for him. Along with this, God has appointed for the servant four rules (qawāʿid), which are of necessity the servant's ecstatic findings (mawājīd) and the mainstay of purposeful striving through insight. They are: encompassment, the good, will, and apprehension. These are four rules; they are the root of roots and the pathway of the intellects. As for encompassment, upon it is built realization, and the return to them is by instruction and by alerting; and whoever ascends by them to the summit of realization has attained human perfection, spiritual deliverance, and the All-Merciful character; and by them he is turned toward what he finds of his own self.

Faṣl. Withdraw into yourself much, and doff your body while alone; and travel as though you were disembodied, without a body, stripped bare of the natural garments, utterly divested of the appurtenances of the body. Then you will be, at that moment, entered into your own essence, gone forth from all things, gathered upon yourself, your mind turned wholly toward you. And you will see in your essence such comeliness, splendour, elevation, and praise as leaves you marvelling, bewildered, dumbfounded. And you will know that you are a part of the highest Omnipotence (jabarūt), a penetrating life, and firmly established goods. From here you become aware of encompassment, and you cleave to love, and you gain might from the centre and the outspreading. And you will see in your essence such light and splendour as you have no strength to witness, nor are you able to take on essential substance (tajawhur) by its being. So you return powerless, the mind dulled, to the world of thought and vision, and you are veiled from that. Then you make yourself ready for the like of that, until you grow familiar with the station, and — praise be to God, exalted is He — no diminution occurs, and contention is lifted from the intelligible content of the returning. /fol. 117v./

Faṣl. It is related from Muqātil b. Sulaymān that he said: Whoever is distressed by some matter, let him perform the ablution amply by night, and let him enter a darkened room, the furthest room in his dwelling, and let him pray to God two rakʿas, completing their bowing and their prostration. Then let him fall down prostrate. Then let him invoke blessing upon the Prophet — God bless him and grant him peace. Then let him say: O God, truly You are a Sovereign, Omnipotent, and whatever You will of the matter comes to be; truly You have power over all things. O God, if my sins have gone before me, and my direction has become confounded, and my offence has grown great, and my errors have multiplied, and they have come between me and the fulfilment of my needs — then truly I ask You by the majesty of Your Face and by the immensity of Your pardon, and I turn toward You by Your prophet Muḥammad — God bless him and grant him peace — that You forgive me, and have mercy upon me, and grant me relief. Then you say, at the top of your voice: O Muḥammad, O Aḥmad, O Abū l-Qāsim! Truly I seek access through you, and I turn by you toward God, mighty and majestic, that He may forgive me, and have mercy upon me, and fulfil my needs, and grant me relief. And if weeping comes upon you, that is the sign that [the prayer] is answered; and if not, then do it again on the second night and on the third, for it is tried-and-tested and sound. Success is from God; and peace.

Faṣl. And it is related from Muqātil b. Sulaymān — and it is an answered supplication, and by it Jesus — peace be upon him — used to bring the dead to life by the leave of God, exalted is He. Muqātil said: I kept seeking it until I found it with a man of religion and righteousness. So, if you wish to pray with it: when you have prayed the dawn prayer, you say — while seated, before you depart from your prayer — one hundred times: In the name of God, the All-Merciful, the Compassionate. There is no power and no strength save in God, the Exalted, the Magnificent. O God, truly I ask You: O Qadīm (Eternal), O Dāʾim (Everlasting), O Fard (Single), O Witr (Odd-numbered), O Aḥad (One), O Ṣamad (Eternal Refuge), O Ḥayy (Living), O Qayyūm (Self-Subsisting), O Possessor of Majesty and Honour! And if you are not answered, then curse Muqātil, whether he be living or dead. So understand.

Faṣl. And whoever is distressed by some matter, or upon whom a distress has fallen touching his religion or his worldly life, in a thing he cannot do without — let him purify himself at sunset on the eve of Friday; then let him seclude himself devotionally for God, mighty and majestic, and let him not speak to anyone until he prays the final night prayer (ʿishāʾ). Then, when he prays the witr, you say in the last prostration of his witr: O Allāh, O Lord, O Ḥayy, O Qayyūm, in You I seek succour, O Allāh — one hundred times; and he asks for his need, and it shall be fulfilled by the leave of God, exalted is He, and by His power.

And it is related from the shaykh, the imām Abū ʿĪsā al-Tirmidhī — may God be pleased with him — from the Prophet — God bless him and grant him peace — that he said: ((When you have a need with God, exalted is He, or with any of the people, then pray two rakʿas and pray with this supplication. You say: There is no god but God, the Forbearing, the Generous. Glory be to God, Lord of the Mighty Throne. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds. I ask You for the things that make Your mercy incumbent, and for the sure resolves of Your forgiveness, and for gain from every act of righteousness, and for safety from every evil. Leave me no sin but that You forgive it, nor any anxiety but that You relieve it, nor any need but that You fulfil it — by Your mercy, O Most Merciful of the merciful.))

And this is a supplication for the fulfilment of needs. It is prayed /fol. 118r./ after praying two rakʿas, with sincerity of intention, and with praise of God, and asking forgiveness, and invoking blessing upon the Messenger of God — God bless him and grant him peace. And you say: O God, O Gatherer of what is scattered, O Bringer-forth of the vegetation, O Reviver of the bones crumbled to dust, O Answerer of supplications, O Fulfiller of needs, O Reliever of distresses, O You who are above the seven heavens, O Opener of the treasuries of bounties, O Owner of the needs of those who ask! Your hearing has heard the voices, and Your knowledge has encompassed every thing. I ask You by Your power over every thing, and by Your independence of the whole of Your creation, and by Your praise, and by Your glory, that You be bounteous to me with my need — and it is such-and-such (and you name it). And you repeat the supplication seven times, or three; and your invocation shall be answered, if God, exalted is He, wills.

Faṣl. ʿAlī — may God ennoble his face — the gate of the city of the knowledge of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, was asked what one should pray with for the fulfilment of needs. He said: You recite six verses from the beginning of Sūrat al-Ḥadīd — All that is in the heavens and what is in the earth glorifies God, and He is the Mighty, the Wise (Q 57:1), up to His words, exalted is He, and He is Knowing of what is within the breasts (Q 57:6) — and the end of Sūrat al-Ḥashr: He is God, other than whom there is no god, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed; He is the All-Merciful, the

Compassionate (Q 59:22), to the end of the sura. Then you say: O You who are thus-and-so, appoint for me in my affair such-and-such, or such — and you mention your need; and it shall be answered for you, if God, exalted is He, wills.

And Abū l-Ḥasan b. Sālim — God have mercy on him — reported, saying: My grandmother had a blindness upon her, so that she could not see. Then one came to her and said to her: Shall I not teach you a name from among the names of God, exalted is He, so that you may pray with it and God will restore your sight to you? She said to him: Yes. He said: Keep it hidden, and tell no one of it. She said: Yes. So he taught it to her and said to her: Spread out your hands, and raise them to heaven, and call upon God, mighty and majestic, by it; then wipe your face with it. So she did, and God restored her sight to her; and she saw before her a shaykh standing, and then he departed from her. And abundant wealth was offered to her on condition that she teach it, but she refused. And at her death she disclosed it to my father. She said to him: Recite Sūrat al-Ḥadīd. So he recited to her the beginning of it, and she said: Part of the Name has passed. Then she said to him: Recite the end of Sūrat al-Ḥashr. So he recited; and when he had finished the end of it, she said: The remainder of the Name has passed. Then she informed him of it.

And ʿAlī — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with him — was asked about the most particular of the names, that with which the Messenger of God — God bless him and grant him peace — had singled him out. He said: I did not think that anyone would ask me about that. Then he said: When you wish to ask God, exalted is He, for a need, then you recite six verses from the beginning of al-Ḥadīd, up to His words, exalted is He, Knower of what is within the breasts (Q 57:6); and from the end of Sūrat al-Ḥashr, from His words, exalted is He, Had We sent down this Qurʾān upon a mountain (Q 59:21), to the end of the sura. Then you say: O You who are thus-and-so, do such-and-such — as has gone before.

And from the supplication of certain of the friends of God (awliyāʾ), namely the shaykh Abū l-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with him. He said: I passed a certain night in great grief, and I was inspired to say: My God, You have graciously bestowed upon me the profession of Your oneness and obedience, yet there have encompassed me /fol. 118v./ appetite, and heedlessness, and disobedience; and the soul has flung me into the sea of wrongdoing. She is the [wronging] one, and Your servant is the wronged, grieved, anxious, sorrowful; and caprice has swallowed him down, and he calls upon You with the call of the divinely preserved one, the imprisoned, Your servant Yūnus b. Mattā, as he says: There is no god but You; glory be to You! Truly I have been among the wrongdoers (Q 21:87). So answer him [Your servant] as You answered him [Yūnus]. And guide me by the might of love in the locus of singling out (tafrīd), of professing oneness, and of unity. And cause to grow up over me the trees of gentle kindness and tenderness, for You are the King, the Tender, the Bountiful Bestower. And I have none but You alone, who have no associate; nor do You break Your promise to whoever believes in You.

For You have said — and Your word is the truth — So We answered him and delivered him from grief; and thus do We deliver the believers (Q 21:88). And may God bless our master Muḥammad and his family and his companions, and grant them peace.

Faṣl. And Muḥammad b. Idrīs said in his Great Book — and that is that the imām Abū l-Qāsim b. Hawāzin al-Qushayrī [readingfor the edition's[ ]mentions] in his Risāla that a merchant, whom Abū l-Qāsim did not name, but whom Muḥammad b. Idrīs named as being Zayd b. Ḥāritha — a brigand wished to kill him, and said to him: Make ready for death. He said to him: Grant me respite until I pray two rakʿas. The brigand said to him: Far from it! Another than you has prayed them, and his prayer did not avail him. So Zayd performed the ablution and prayed two rakʿas, and supplicated with this supplication: O Wadūd (the Loving), O Wadūd, O Possessor of the Glorious Throne, O Doer of what He wills! I ask You by the light of Your face, which has filled the pillars of Your Throne. I ask You by [Your power], whereby You have power over all Your creation, and by Your mercy, which embraces all things. O Mughīth (the Succourer), succour me! O Mughīth, succour me! O Mughīth, by Your power succour me! — 3 [times]. He supplicated with it 3 times. Then the brigand came at him and raised his spear to strike him — and behold, a horseman had come, coursing over the ground, and he was calling out: Do not kill him! So he turned about, and saw that the horseman had come, and in his hand was a spear; and he struck him with it and felled him — by his ear — from the top of his mount, so that he dropped to the ground. Then he turned to Zayd and said to him: O Zayd, go forward to him and kill him. Zayd said to him: I do not kill anyone. So the horseman went back to him and killed him. Then he said: O Zayd, when you supplicated the first time, behold, Jibrīl was saying: Who is for this anguished one? I said: I am. And I was in the seventh heaven. And when you supplicated the second time, I was in the nearest heaven. And when you supplicated the third time, I came to you. And know, O Zayd, that no one supplicates with the like of that with which you supplicated but that he is answered as you have been answered. And when Zayd returned to Medina and informed the Messenger of God — God bless him and grant him peace — of the report, he said to him: O Zayd, God has taught you the Greatest Name, by which, when He is called upon, He answers, and when He is asked by it, He gives. And Muḥammad b. Idrīs set it under the chapter-heading "The names that shake the angels". And God knows best.

Faṣl, in which I mention a ḥālūma [a dream-oracle] — by God, a wondrous request for guidance (istikhāra). If you wish to know the outcome of an affair, and how the way out of it lies, you pray two rakʿas after the final ʿishāʾ prayer, with three taslīms: in the first, with al-Ḥamd (the Fātiḥa) and al-Ḍuḥā; and in the second, with By the fig and the olive (Q 95:1); and in the third, with Have We not expanded your breast for you (Q 94:1), after the Mother of the Qurʾān; and in the fourth, with al-Ḥamd and Truly We sent it down on the Night of Power (Q 97:1); and in the fifth, with al-Ḥamd and When the earth is shaken (Q 99:1); and in the sixth, with al-Ḥamd and Say: He is God,

One (Q 112:1). Then, when you have finished /fol. 119r./ your prayer, you write upon a written petition (barāʾa): "To the Lord, the Majestic, the Generous, the Loving, the Mighty, the Compeller, the Supremely Great — from His servant So-and-so son of So-and-so, the servant, poor, lowly, needy, wretched, a beggar driven by necessity, who has found none for his need but You. He seeks and desires from You such-and-such a need" — and he names it. "O God, truly I ask You — O Lord, O Allāh, O Ḥayy (the Living), O Ghanī (the Self-Sufficient), O Karīm (the Generous), O Qawī (the Strong), O Qadīr (the All-Powerful) — Your servant, the weak, the poor, the wretched, seeks and desires from You such-and-such. O God, truly I ask You by every name that is Yours, by which You have named Yourself, or which You have sent down in Your Book, or which You have taught to any of Your creation, or which You have kept to Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen with You: that You appoint for me, out of my affair, a relief and a way out, and a healing clarification, and that You fulfil my need." And you mention whatever you wish — the turning of a heart toward you, or affection, or love and mercy toward you — and the clarification of what has been hard for you to understand, and if you wish, [a request] to be brought to knowledge of the outcome of his affair and the clarification of its time. Then you fumigate your writing with grains of good male frankincense, and you fold it and seal it with wax — white, raw, and new. Then you cast the petition into running water. And if you place the petition in a tube (juʿba) of Persian reed and seal the mouth of the tube with the white wax — the tube being marked (manʿūta) at its base, bound with a stout thread — and you tie it to a tree or to a peg and let the tube trail in the running water, and you say: I have set flowing the heart of So-and-so son of So-and-so [f.]. And for this also: that you place it in a vessel of water and set it at your head, and sleep in a state of ritual purity and ablution; for your need and what you seek will be represented to you. And there is no power and no strength save in God, the High, the Mighty.

Faṣl. And this supplication is related from ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Zayd al-Qayrawānī — may God, exalted is He, have mercy upon him — that he said: I have seen many supplications, but I have neither seen nor tried any swifter in the answer, nor mightier, than this supplication. And it is that with which the shaykh, the jurist Abū Isḥāq al-Tūnisī, used to supplicate against every tyrannical sultan, and against every aggressive brigand, and every calamity and hardship and misfortune. So whoever comes upon it, let him guard it well, for it is the supplication of the elect; and let none but the godfearing supplicate with it, for it is tried-and-tested and sound. And it is this supplication: O God, O Place of every complaint, O Witness of every secret converse, O Knower of every hidden thing, O You who remove what You will of every affliction! O Moses the Confidant (najī), O Muḥammad the Chosen (muṣṭafā), and Abraham the Intimate Friend (khalīl) — the blessings of God and His peace be upon them all! I call upon You, O my God, with the call of one whose destitution has grown severe, and whose strength has weakened, and whose expedients have grown few — the call of the stranger, the drowning, the anguished, the distressed, who finds none to remove what afflicts him but You. There is no god but You, O Most Merciful of the merciful! Remove what has come down upon us from Your enemy and our enemy, the accursed Satan, and from these wrongdoing folk — or So-and-so, if it be a single person. O Lord of the worlds, truly You have power over all things. O for succour! /fol. 119v./ O for succour! O for succour! O Allāh, O Allāh, O Allāh! O for succour, O Allāh! O God, O Initiator who has no beginning, O Everlasting who has no ending, O Ḥayy, O Reviver of the dead, O You who stand over every soul for what it has earned! O God, You are God: there is no god but You, one God. I ask You, by the perfect words, for security and pardon and well-being in this world and the next, and in family and body and wealth and children, and for all the Muslims. O Lord of the worlds, truly You have power over all things. So have mercy upon me by Your mercy, O Most Merciful of the merciful, and remove from me what has come down upon me of every anxiety and harm — and whatever [else] you wish — and deliver me with a goodly deliverance. And make your intention toward God, exalted is He, good, for the benefits lie in the beliefs. And may God bless our master Muḥammad and his family and his companions, and grant them peace. And God speaks the truth, and He guides to the way.

Faṣl. Know — may God grant me and you success in obeying Him and in the understanding of the secrets of His names — that the secret of the letters is inscribed upon the tablets of the breasts of the learned; and the secret of the Night Journey (al-isrāʾ) is traced out upon the pages of the thoughts of the sages; and the secret of alchemy is stored up in the enclosure of the treasure of the ancients; and the secret of subjugation is hidden away in the horizons of the hearts of the friends of God; and the secret of the names is set down in symbol in the mirror of the excellence of the prophets; and the secret of speech is laid up as treasure in the throne of the heaven of the spirits. So understand these Throne-expressions and holy indications, these subtleties of unveiling and gnoses of divine bestowal, and you will win an ample portion of the meanings that come of [spiritual] tasting and of the oft-repeated strains of longing. And God speaks the truth, and He guides to the way.

And know that every invocation by one of the names has a gate through which it enters, and a ladder of ascent (miʿrāj) by which it climbs, and a spiritual being that ascends with it, and a terminus at which the invocation halts; and the answer comes forth from that gate, and descends by that ladder of ascent, at the hands of those angels, and at that [same] time — if the answer be hastened — or at the like of it among the hours. So understand that. Know — may God teach you the realities of the names and grant you provision from the degrees of enumeration (iḥṣāʾ) — that, since the stations of religion are three stations, the station of islām and the station of faith (īmān) and the station of excellence (iḥsān); and the degrees of the gardens, ordered according to the enumeration, are for the people of religion three, the Garden of Works and the Garden of Inheritance and the Garden of Gracious Bestowal; and since the kinds of enumeration are three — attachment (taʿalluq) in the station of islām, assimilation of character (takhalluq) in the station of faith, and realization (taḥaqquq) in the station of excellence — therefore their enumeration by attachment, in the station of islām, is that the wayfarer should seek out the traces of each one of these names in his soul and his body and all his faculties, or his limbs and his parts, and in all his states and his constitution, psychic and corporeal, and in his forbearance, his innate dispositions, and the kinds of his purifications; so that he sees all that as belonging to the determinations of these names and to their traces. Let him then meet every trace with what befits it — as blessings are met with thanksgiving, and afflictions with patience, and so forth. /fol. 120r./ And enumeration of this sort falls under the Garden of Works, which is the locus of the secret of the passing accidents [exchanged] for the fixed, abiding entities; and it is that of which Abraham the Intimate Friend — peace be upon him — gave tidings, that it is level plains, and that its planting is "Glory be to God" and "Praise be to God". And their enumeration by assimilation of character, in the station of faith, is the straining upward of the spiritual soul toward the realities of these names and their meanings and what is understood of them, and the assimilation of the character of each name among them, after the manner of what is reported of his words — upon him be blessing and peace: ((Assume the character traits of God, exalted is He.)) — such that that assimilation of character is from that name, that is to say, there is produced in response to him what is produced in response to that name. And by the like of this enumeration this assimilation of character enters the Garden of Inheritance, which is higher than the first Garden — rather, it is its inward, descending from it, standing to it as the world of the Dominion (malakūt) stands to the world of the Kingdom (mulk); and it is that to which reference is made in his words — upon him be blessing and peace: ((There is not one of you but that he has his dwelling in the Garden and his dwelling in the Fire. So when he dies and enters the Fire, the people of the Garden inherit his dwelling; and when he dies and enters the Garden, the people of the Fire inherit his dwelling. And if you wish, recite: Those are the inheritors, who shall inherit Paradise; therein they shall abide forever (Q 23:10–11).)) And their enumeration by realization, in the station of excellence, is by transferences and by the stripping off of whatever subsists in you and appears in you of the forms and the meanings — the naming being the naming of temporal origination — and by [concealment within] the Presence of the Real, veiled behind its veils and its entities [readingfor the edition's
, with MS B's
.] And God knows best.
Verse
I veiled myself from my age beneath the shadow of His wing, so that I see my age and it does not see me.
Were you to ask the days what my name is, they would not know; and where my place is, they would not know my place.

An enumeration such as this brings the one who assimilates the character [of the names] into the Garden of Gracious Bestowal, which is the locus of the secret of the Unseen, the very [garden] alluded to in his saying — upon him be blessing and peace: ((Therein is what no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it ever occurred to the heart of any mortal.))

And to it too is the allusion in His saying, exalted is He: Truly the God-fearing shall be amid gardens and a river, in a seat of truthfulness, in the presence of an all-powerful Sovereign (Q 54:54–55). I say: seeing that the righteous forebears did not ascend to the realities of the Dominion (al-malakūt) and the wonders of the Omnipotence (al-jabarūt) save by realizing the assimilation of character through the names, until every name is transformed, in the most rightful [state] of its station, into something mightier by reason of what he sees of the gifts of God, exalted is He, and of the subtleties of the [divine] wisdoms. And whenever you hear [mention of] the Greatest Name upon the tongue of this company, this is its reality. And when they have brought the names to perfection, the names return to them as mighty names; and that is in the perfection of the stations and the attainment of the ultimate ends. So there remains for them no name by which they may wayfare toward creation; rather they are made pure in the Name of the Essence, which is the reality of the assimilation of character, and it is "Allāh"; and by it the Command came to pass. He said, exalted is He: Say: "God" — then leave them to their idle discourse, playing (Q 6:91). Then, beyond doubt, although the [devotional] works — according to the difference of their aims and the striving of the gnostics in their phases /fol. 120v./ — do bring one to the purification of hearts, to the beginnings of charismatic graces (karāmāt), and to the transformation of states, yet as for those who wayfare upon the path of the names and the ladders of ascent, there are unveiled to them the secrets of the Dominion and the perplexities of faith in the swiftest time and the nearest span; and there appear upon them the lights of the [divine] wisdoms, together with the subtleties of the sciences and the realities of the gnoses of the Dominion, given by [God's] bestowal. And that is by reason of aiming at the path with verification, and of wayfaring with sincerity and affirmation.

Faṣl. Men have differed concerning the name (ism): is it derived from al-sumūw (elevation) or from al-sima (the mark)? In that there is a subtle indication for the possessors of the realities — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with them — namely, that those who journey to God, exalted is He, are of two classes: a murād (one divinely willed), stationed; or a murīd (an aspirant), upstanding. As for the upstanding aspirant, every name that he undertakes binds him to be qualified by it outwardly and inwardly; so the name, in his regard, is a wasm (a brand), because it brands the station by it, and thus [the word ism] would be taken from wasm. But if he be a murād, or ascend to the degree of the murād, then the names raise him up while he himself is still, by reason of his absorption in the witnessing of the lights of the theophany (tajallī) within the meanings of the names. So his rank is elevated above wayfaring by means of the names, and that name, in his regard, becomes sumūw (elevation), taken from samā … sumūwan, [said] when a thing rises high. An indication concerning the manifestation of the names: namely, that the final issue in the hereafter is unto subsistence, whereas the final issue in the abode of this world is unto annihilation; so your attributes in this world are perishing in respect of their attribution. Therefore God has graciously bestowed upon you His subsisting names, that you might witness by their realities the promised subsistence within the witnessed annihilation — as al-Ṣiddīq, may God, exalted is He, be pleased with him, said: "Were the veil to be lifted, I would not increase in certainty." And beware lest you call upon Him by your own names, for then you would be calling upon the Subsisting by means of the perishing; for if you subsist through yourself, you subsist through one who once was not, whereas if you subsist through Him, you subsist through One who has never ceased to be. How far apart, then, are the two names, and how distant the two judgements! And God, exalted is He, said: So flee unto God; truly I am to you, from Him, a clear warner (Q 51:50). "So flee unto God" — that is, from your own selves and from the names of your attributes. And He said, exalted is He: To God belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them (Q 7:180). Another indication: namely, that God, exalted is He, made mention of you in His pre-eternity — nay, in His post-eternity — by your own most beautiful names, where He said, exalted is He: Truly the men who submit and the women who submit, and the believing men and the believing women (Q 33:35), to the end of the verse. Then He commanded you to make mention of Him by His Most Beautiful Names, whereupon your reality was bewildered in the seas of passionate distraction and your intellect strayed in the wastelands of incapacity. So He had mercy upon you by the guide of subtle kindness and the leader of mercy and compassion, and said, exalted is He: He is God, other than whom there is no god: the King, the All-Holy, the Peace, the Granter of Security, the Overseer, the Mighty, the Compeller, the

Supremely Great (Q 59:23), to the end of the verse. So be qualified by the best of your names, by which He named you, for they are His gracious favour; and then His Most Beautiful Names, which are His mercy, will be called to mind — an allusion to /fol. 121r./ His saying, exalted is He: So glorify the name of your Lord, the Magnificent (Q 56:74). And glorification (tasbīḥ) is the prayer, and the prayer is glorification; for the name of a thing has been made to speak for the thing itself, in the sense of proximity. That is: pray by the secret of glorification, whose reality is the declaring [of God] transcendent above every originated attribute. So the name derived from it [i.e. from ṣalāt] is ṣila (a bond); and [it is taken also] in the sense of the thing named, according to the way of him who distinguishes between the name and the named. So the glorification of God — that is, the declaring of Him transcendent — is at one time by utterance and at another by belief; and that is not sound save after the establishment of gnosis, the unveiling of the secrets of the proof, annihilation in the affirmation of [God's] uniqueness (tafrīd), and realization in divestment (tajrīd). And that is sound only for the people of the Real, who have known Him by the qualities of majesty and described Him by the kinds of perfection, and so have surrendered Lordship to Him and cast their own essences into the bond of servanthood before Him. Nor is the glorification of God sound from you until you declare your soul free of every blameworthy appetite, and your faith of the works of deficiency, and your intellect of caprice, and your spirit of turning toward familiar things, and your heart of the darkness of moments of heedlessness, and your body of habits and transgressions and of eating what is forbidden and what is doubtful. And then there will appear to you every name among the names of the attributes of the Essence, and every name among the names of the attributes of the Acts, and every name among the names of the meanings — mighty in itself, great in its worth. Of this is what is related of Ibrāhīm al-Khawwāṣ— may God, exalted is He, be pleased with him. He said: I had stripped from my inmost being the love of appetites, save the love of pomegranates. I passed by a man afflicted with a severe malady, with hornets settling upon him and devouring his flesh. I greeted him with peace, and he returned the greeting to me; then he named me by my name, without any prior acquaintance. So I came forward and said: I see that you have a state with God, exalted is He; if only you would call upon Him, He would deliver you from these hornets. He said: And I see that you have a state with God, exalted is He, O Ibrāhīm; if only you would call upon Him, He would deliver you from the appetite for pomegranates — for the sting of the hornets is upon bodies, but the sting of the appetites is upon hearts. This, then, is the discipline of words. And among them is he who observed [this] discipline by the striking of a similitude, as is related of one of them. He said: I saw a young man, upon whom was a cloak and in whose hand was a leather water-vessel, and he said to me: I am a man who aims at scrupulousness, and so I eat nothing but what people cast away; and it may be that I find the peel of something to which the ants have got before me — shall I cast it away, or shall I eat it? Is there anything [of blame] upon me in that? He said: So I said within myself: There is none upon the earth who is scrupulous in a matter such as this — as one who disapproved.

He said: Then I looked at him, and behold, the man was standing upon ground of pure silver. And he said to me: Riches are forbidden — and he vanished from my sight. These, then, are they whose secrets God has guarded and whose litanies of remembrance He has purified and whose inner sights He has illumined, so that they have come to know the secret of the names, and the glorification that belongs to them, and the declaring [of God] transcendent, and the holding oneself aloof within the lights of witnessing them; and the magnification of the meanings of the names has been made luminous to them, inasmuch as they witness the lights of their meanings.

Tanbīh (an admonition). Glorification (tasbīḥ) is a tafʿīl form from al-sabḥ, and al-sabḥis the coming and the going. God, exalted is He, said: Truly you have in the daytime a long going to and fro (Q 73:7) — that is, a coming and a going. /fol. 121v./ And one of the gnostics said: The glorifier glorifies by an inward secret whose reality is the purity of the qualities of his thought, in the arena of the wonders of the Dominion and the subtleties of the realities of the Omnipotence. The wayfarer glorifies by his litany of remembrance in the seas of the heart; the aspirant glorifies by his heart in the seas of thought; the lover glorifies by his spirit in the seas of longing; the gnostic glorifies by his secret in the seas of the Unseen; and the veracious one (ṣiddīq) glorifies by the secret of his secret in the secret of the seas of the most holy lights that issue forth in the meanings of the names of the attributes, together with the firm planting of the feet of empowerment amid the variation of states. So understand that with a verification of the utmost degree of witnessing. The witnessing of every wayfarer, [drawn] from the presences of the names, is none other than the name which is his vision — that is, the name from whose presence this wayfarer has issued forth. And by his witnessing there accrues to him complete knowledge of what has attached to him from the presences of the names; and his witnessing of it is not complete so long as that witnessing is not granted him by that incapacity and bewilderment within the object witnessed, such that his expression of it is [only] implicit and his apprehension of it is incapacity. And hence the most expansive of creation in witnessing says: ((I cannot enumerate praise of You)), and says: ((O God, increase me in bewilderment concerning You)). Lāʾiḥa (a flash of insight). It lies with the speaker to say that there is, among the Most Beautiful Names of God, no name of the Essence except His name, exalted is He, "Allāh", and that alone; since the name of the Essence is an expression for that which is posited for the reality itself, without regard to any superadded meaning, and we possess nothing that is so save this name. And it may [also] be said that the Essence has no expression indicating it apart from our own regarding it under some one of the regards, at all. Each of these two positions has an aspect [of soundness], provided it proceeds from a complete aspect and a penetrating insight. And God is the Granter of success unto the [right] purposes, through acquaintance with the aims of the people of the Real. May God, exalted is He, make us of them.

Faṣl. Know that the names of the Acts are of two kinds. One kind is that concerning which the Law has mentioned the act without the name, such as "the displeasure of God", "the wrath of God", "the curse of God", and "the bounty of God". And one kind is that concerning which the Law has mentioned them both together, as in His saying: God creates what He wills (Q 24:45), and God is the Creator of all things (Q 39:62), and the like of that.

Tanbīh. Know that these realities of His names are of two kinds. One kind has no outward verbal form to indicate it to us, and to it is the allusion in his saying — God bless him and grant him peace: ((O God, truly I ask You by every name that is Yours, by which You have named Yourself, or which You have sent down in Your Book, or which You have taught to any one of Your creatures, or which You have kept to Yourself in the hidden store of the Unseen with You.)) And the second kind is that which has with us an outward form, verbal or written, which is the name that indicates it to us. And that is of two divisions. The first of them is implicit (muḍmar), such as the expression "He", and "I", and "We", and the kāf of address and its tāʾ, and the pronoun of the absent person and of the plural. And the second division is explicit (muẓhar), such as the expression "Allāh", and al-ʿAlīm (the All-Knowing), and al-Khāliq (the Creator), and their like. So understand — and God is the Granter of success. Faṣl. Know that the existence of every person, human or otherwise, is referred back to a name, universal or particular, among the divine names. So understand that, and you will win the hidden secret and the treasured knowledge by unveiling. And that is because He — glorified and exalted is He — has men who are the men of the names: they are ninety-nine men, together with one all-comprehending man who is called the Ghawth (the Succour), the Singular, the Quṭb (the Pole), the All-Comprehending. Not one of these /fol. 122r./ ninety-nine men knows him, although

— their all drawing their sustaining supply from him at root. And whenever any one of the names of God, exalted is He, agrees with a personal name (ism dhāt) in the letter-number and the numerical [value] and in its breaking, and its wafq agrees, then that is a Greatest Name in respect of that person: by means of it there is acted upon for him whatever is acted upon by the Greatest Name that is sought. So understand that, for I have not the power to speak plainly, since the disclosure of it is not permitted. And I heard one of the masters who are gnostics say that every supplicant who calls upon God, exalted is He, has a name that is, in relation to him, the greatest of the names — just as Arḥam al-Rāḥimīn (the Most Merciful of the merciful) was for Job, and al-Wahhāb (the Bestower) for Solomon, and Khayr al-Wārithīn (the Best of inheritors) for Zechariah, and "There is no god but You; glory be to You; truly I was among the wrongdoers" (cf. Q 21:87) for Jonah. And this is according to the state of the one who supplicates, and not according to what is asked and sought by the supplication. And this saying is close to the [true] sense, and it is the saying of the generality of our Sufi masters and of those who wayfare the path of realization and gravity. And I say: the shaykh, the imām, the gnostic of God, the erudite Muḥammad al-Khwārizmī — may God, exalted is He, sanctify his inmost secret — said, in the sacred precinct of Mecca, in the year six hundred and seventy: Whoever knows God, exalted is He, by the odd name (al-witr) in his state and his station has come to know the Greatest Name that is proper to him. And know that God, glorified and exalted, out of His subtle kindness, has made His names manifest as varied in composition, so that each name among them may indicate one kind among the kinds of His acts and His ways, and so that every wayfarer may find an easy path befitting him. So that will be the Greatest Name befitting him in his aim, for his state, once he knows it and asks by it at every time that is suited to the name. Thus there comes together — out of the knowledge of the time, the knowledge of the proportional relations, the knowledge of the name befitting the time, and the need that corresponds to the name at that time, together with the turning of the heart toward that particular kind that is sought —

above all, the swiftness of the answer. For whoever supplicates according to this rule is answered on the instant. And in that is an allusion to the hadith of the Messenger of God — God bless him and grant him peace: ((Truly God has, in the days of your age, wafts of grace; lo, lay yourselves open to them.)) For the wafts are the coinciding of the time befitting the thing sought and of the name that corresponds to the object of intent. And this kind of secrets was unveiled to the people of God's providential care from among the messengers and His servants brought near; and for that reason the answer was swift in their case.

Faṣl. And know that the comprehensive secret and the decisive unveiling in supplication is that you take the number of the letters of the names by which you make remembrance — the example being your saying al-Laṭīf al-Khabīr (the Subtle, the All-Aware). And do not take the definite article (ālat al-taʿrīf, i.e. the al-); rather you take Laṭīf Khabīr. And you look at how many numbers belong to the two of them according to the masters of the secrets, and you multiply them by the days of the week, up to the utmost amount. Then make remembrance of it in a state of purity and prayer, with concentration of aspiration (himma) and purity of the inward, in a place empty of sounds; for you will find the secret of the answer at that very time. So ponder it, for it is of the red sulphur and the greatest theriac. And one of the great ones /fol. 122v./ among the people of inner sight said: Know that the guarded secret and the hidden knowledge in the litany of remembrance by the names is that you take the number of the letters of the names and the number of their numerical forms, which are what you make remembrance of. An example of that: the name of God, exalted is He, [Allāh] is four letters, and it has, in number, sixty-six; so the sum of that is 70. So you cry to Him for help by it 70 times, then you ask your need. Then you return and say likewise, according to the number of the name of the need, in an empty place, with concentration of aspiration and presence of heart; for it will be answered for you at that very moment and time. So ponder it, for it is of the treasured secrets and the hidden, guarded jewels, by the leave of God, exalted is He.

And know that every name has an occult property which it does not overstep, nor does the one who makes remembrance by it pass beyond it to any other. So ponder it, for it is God's secret in the visible kingdom (mulk) and the Dominion (malakūt); and you will never find in God's wont any alteration (cf. Q 33:62; 48:23). And know that among the names there is that whose occult property is in it alone, not found in any other, because of its narrowness; and among them there are those in which two names, or three, come together in a single meaning. And in this is a wondrous secret and a strange matter. So glory be to God, al-ʿAlīm (the All-Knowing), al-Ḥakīm (the Wise). And know that the occult properties of every name are from what is derived from it, and the operative deployment by it is from what it requires. And this is the recondite secret which is opened only to every servant who turns [to God] in penitence: And none is granted it save those who have been patient; and none is granted it save the possessor of a mighty portion (Q 41:35). And whoever has a door opened to him in that has won an abundant portion of the knowledge of the Family of Muḥammad.

Faṣl. Know that every name of the names of God, exalted is He: if its letters are odd [in number], it is suitable for separation and dispersal; and if they are even, it is suitable for joining, for pairing, for love, and for affection. And know that every name has letters and numbers, and every number has a wafq. So whoever gathers, out of the letters of every name and the number of what is in every square, is granted success to the unveiling of the secret. And every one of the names has a spiritual being (rūḥānī) which the configured air endows with its body. I have refrained from mentioning that, because of what it involves of the disclosure of the secret and of grave peril; and had I known that it would not become manifest to anyone [else], I would have brought forth from it the strange secrets and the wondrous matters. And for whoever has provision decreed for him, I would have brought forth from it the like of the form of the attracting magnet and of the procuring ruby, from mouth to mouth. He casts the Spirit, of His command, upon whomever He wills of His servants (Q 40:15). So swim, if you are a swimmer; and roam, if you are a rover. For this is the pearl of allusions, come forth within the shells of expressions; and the realities of the celestial things have descended into the dwelling-places of the terrestrial things. So buy her for a small price before she slips away, and expend the very substance of what you have hoarded as her bridal dower, before the drinking of the cups of regret from the wine-jars of "Our Lord, send us back, that we may do righteous work other than what we used to do" (cf. Q 35:37), and you find yourself upon the carpet of abasement at the terrifying cry of Did We not give you a life long enough for whoever would take heed to take heed therein? And the warner came to you (Q 35:37). Oh, what a clattering — how mighty its closing in! And what a trial — how bitter its taste! So understand this matter /fol. 123r./ and ponder this reminder: Truly God causes to hear whomever He wills; and you cannot make those in the graves hear. You are only a warner (Q 35:22–23). And if the one who considers would but think and deal fairly, he would gain magnificent sciences. And God speaks the truth, and He guides to the way.

Khātima (conclusion). Know — may God, exalted is He, grant us and you the success of the gnostics, and guide us and you with the guidance of the aspirants — that the conditions for the operation with the names, with the litany of remembrance, and with the invocations are very many indeed; but among them are those that are indispensable for everyone, and among them are those that are a condition in respect of some and not others. And here I am — if God, exalted is He, wills — to mention to you all of that, each in a faṣl proper to it.
